title: DRESS & AGEP (severe drug reactions)
summary: Two severe cutaneous adverse reactions that are easy to miss: DRESS (late-onset rash, fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia and organ damage) and AGEP (sudden sheets of tiny sterile pustules within days of a drug).

glance.think: A widespread rash with fever 2–8 weeks after a new drug (DRESS), or sudden pinhead pustules in the folds within days (AGEP).
glance.engine: T-cell mediated reactions, with viral (HHV-6) reactivation in DRESS and neutrophil recruitment in AGEP.
glance.backbone: Stop the culprit and arrange same-day hospital assessment; bloods for eosinophils, LFTs, renal function; lifelong avoidance and alert.
glance.never_miss: Liver, kidney, lung or heart involvement in DRESS; misdiagnosing AGEP as pustular psoriasis or infection.

list: **DRESS** (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms; also called DIHS): a delayed, multi-organ reaction with fever, rash and internal organ involvement. Mortality ~**2–10%**.
**AGEP** (acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis): an abrupt eruption of **sterile, non-follicular pinhead pustules** on oedematous erythema. Usually self-limiting; mortality <5%.

**DRESS:** type IVb (Th2/eosinophils) with **sequential herpesvirus reactivation** (HHV-6, then EBV/CMV), which explains the relapsing course. Culprits: **allopurinol**, **carbamazepine**, phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, **sulfonamides/dapsone**, minocycline, vancomycin, abacavir/nevirapine, strontium. Latency **2–8 weeks** (long).

**AGEP:** type IVd (T cells → IL-8 → neutrophils). Culprits: **aminopenicillins**, macrolides, cephalosporins, **pristinamycin**, **hydroxychloroquine**, **diltiazem**, terbinafine. Latency **<48 h** (antibiotics) — up to 1–2 weeks for some drugs. IL36RN variants overlap with generalised pustular psoriasis.

head: DRESS
AGEP
rows: Morbilliform, becomes infiltrated/oedematous, **>50% BSA**; **facial oedema** (key sign); may become exfoliative
Pinhead pustules on erythema, starting in **flexures/face** and becoming generalised; burning/itch
**Lymphadenopathy**, eosinophilia (>1.5), atypical lymphocytes; **organ involvement — liver (commonest), kidney, lung, heart (myocarditis), thyroid**
Weeks–months; relapses; **late autoimmune disease** (thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes)

diagnosis: FBC with differential and film, LFT, U&E, urinalysis, troponin/ECG if symptomatic, TFT, lipase, HHV-6 PCR, skin biopsy. AGEP: biopsy shows subcorneal/intraepidermal spongiform pustules (to distinguish it from pustular psoriasis). Patch testing later (useful for both).
differentials: DRESS: viral exanthem, lymphoma (especially angioimmunoblastic), hypereosinophilic syndrome, SJS/TEN, Kawasaki disease. AGEP: **generalised pustular psoriasis** (history of psoriasis, slower onset, longer course), subcorneal pustular dermatosis, pustular DRESS, folliculitis, SJS/TEN (early AGEP can show Nikolsky-like sloughing).

list: **Stop the culprit**, document, Yellow Card, and avoid for life (including cross-reacting drugs).

**DRESS:** Same-day hospital assessment if fever/facial oedema/eosinophilia or abnormal LFTs; Mild disease without significant organ involvement: potent topical steroids; With organ involvement: **systemic corticosteroids** (e.g. prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day) **tapered slowly over 6–12 weeks** — rapid tapers cause relapse; Monitor organs for months, and check **TFT/glucose** for 1–2 years
**AGEP:** stop the drug; potent TCS; antipyretics; supportive care. Systemic steroids are rarely needed. Usually managed in dermatology or with admission if unwell.

management: Fever + rash + facial oedema/lymphadenopathy 2–8 weeks after a new anticonvulsant/allopurinol/sulfonamide → same-day admission (check FBC/LFT/U&E). Widespread pustules within days of an antibiotic → same-day dermatology.
Recognise, stop, refer, document, Yellow Card. After discharge: support the specialist steroid taper (steroid card if prolonged), and monitor TFT/glucose per the specialist letter.
red_flags: Suspected DRESS: **same-day** hospital assessment, because hepatitis, nephritis and myocarditis can follow.
Allopurinol (HLA-B*58:01), carbamazepine (HLA-B*15:02) and lamotrigine are high-risk starts: counsel to report a rash early.
pearls: DRESS has the **longest latency** of the SCARs (2–8 weeks), and AGEP the shortest (hours–2 days).
"**Allopurinol + CKD + recent start + rash** = DRESS/SJS risk" — dose adjustment and HLA-B*58:01 awareness.
